title: Resolving conflicts
examples: How can I use I-statements when my friend is always late?
What is the difference between listening and just waiting to speak?
If we disagree on a group project, how do we find common ground?

explain.say: Today we are learning about resolving conflicts with others.

items: I-statements help you talk about your feelings.
They focus on how you feel, not what others did.
Structure: I feel [emotion] when you [action] because [reason].

explain.say: For example, instead of saying you are annoying, try this.

draw.text: I feel sad when you take my pencil.

explain.say: Next, good listening means hearing the whole message fully.

draw.text: Active Listening: Hearing the whole message.

explain.say: A concrete example of listening is repeating back what you heard.
Finding common ground means seeing what you both agree on.
In real life, if you and a friend want different snacks, you can find common ground.

faq.q: What is the difference between an I-statement and a blaming statement?
faq.a: An I-statement focuses on your feelings, like saying I feel upset. A blaming statement points fingers, like saying you always make me upset. You can also ask, 'How do I make it about me?'
asks: How do I stop blaming people?
What is the difference between 'you' and 'I' statements?

faq.q: When should I use an I-statement?
faq.a: You should use them when you feel upset about something someone did. It helps you express yourself calmly. You might also ask, 'Is it okay to use I-statements at school?'
asks: When is it best to use 'I feel'?
Can I use this for small things too?

faq.q: How do I know if I am really listening?
faq.a: You know you are listening by summarizing what the other person said. Try saying, 'So, if I hear you right, you mean...'. You could also ask, 'What does good listening look like in practice?'
asks: Do I need to agree to listen well?

faq.q: If we can't find common ground, what should we do?
faq.a: If you cannot find common ground, you should take a short break to cool down. Then, you can try listing one thing you both value. You might ask, 'What if we just take a break first?'
asks: How do I pause a disagreement?

faq.q: What does 'finding common ground' really mean?
faq.a: It means finding an area of agreement even if you disagree on other things. It is about the shared goal, not the details. You could ask, 'Can we list our shared goals?'
asks: Is common ground the same as compromise?
How do I find something we both like?

faq.q: Why is it important to use I-statements?
faq.a: Because they make people less defensive and help solve the actual problem. They keep the focus on the behavior, not the person. You might ask, 'Are I-statements always polite?'
asks: Does using 'I' make me sound weak?
Can I use this when I am very angry?

faq.q: What are the rules for good listening?
faq.a: The rules are to pay attention, not interrupt, and to reflect back what you heard. This shows respect for the speaker. You could ask, 'What if I am distracted?'
asks: Should I nod my head while listening?
Is it okay to look at my phone while listening?

facts: I-statements use the structure: I feel [emotion] when you [action].
Active listening involves paraphrasing to confirm understanding.
Finding common ground means identifying shared interests or goals.
Using 'I' statements keeps the conversation focused on feelings.

quiz.say: Instead of saying, 'You never clean your room,' you should say:
quiz.show: I feel frustrated when your room is messy.

options.show: I feel frustrated when your room is messy.
options.say: I feel frustrated when your room is messy.

options.show: I am frustrated by your mess.
options.say: I am frustrated by your mess.

options.show: When you are messy, I get frustrated.
options.say: When you are messy, I get frustrated.

quiz.why: This uses the correct structure focusing on your feeling and the action.

wrong.1: This is a generalization that blames the person.
wrong.2: This is too vague and does not state the specific action.
wrong.3: This is better, but the direct 'I feel' structure is stronger.

quiz.say: If your partner wants to play soccer and you want to read a book, what is a good common ground?

options.show: You should just read your book.
options.say: You should just read your book.

options.show: Neither of us can do anything.
options.say: Neither of us can do anything.

options.show: We can play soccer for thirty minutes and then I can read.
options.say: We can play soccer for thirty minutes and then I can read.

quiz.why: This suggests a compromise that meets both needs partially.

wrong.0: This dismisses the other person's interest completely.
wrong.1: This gives up on finding any solution at all.
wrong.3: This ignores your desire to read a book entirely.

quiz.say: When someone tells you a long story, what is the best thing to do first?

options.show: Look at my phone while they talk.
options.say: Look at my phone while they talk.

quiz.why: Good listening requires giving the speaker your full, uninterrupted attention.

wrong.1: This shows you were more interested in speaking than hearing.
wrong.2: You might miss details if you try to summarize too soon.
wrong.3: This sends a non-verbal message that you do not care.
